en: Welcome to our home. We are so happy you could come.
tamil: எங்க வீட்டுக்கு வரவேற்கிறோம். நீங்க வந்தது ரொம்ப சந்தோஷம்.
context: Greeting guests arriving for a house-warming.
explain: 'We are happy you could come' shows the guests are valued.
usage: Say it at the door when guests arrive for a function at your house.
leelaQ: How do you feel when guests come to your home?
answer: I feel very happy and a little busy.

en: Congratulations on your new house, it is really spacious.
tamil: புது வீட்டுக்கு வாழ்த்துகள், இது ரொம்ப விசாலமா இருக்கு.
context: Visiting a friend's house-warming ceremony.
explain: 'Spacious' means having a lot of room inside.
usage: Say it to a friend who has just moved into a new home.
leelaQ: What kind of house would you like to live in?
answer: I would like a small house with a garden.

en: Sorry to bother you, but do you have a pen I could borrow?
tamil: தொந்தரவுக்கு மன்னிக்கணும், நான் வாங்கிக்கற மாதிரி உங்ககிட்ட பேனா இருக்கா?
context: Asking a stranger for a pen at a function.
explain: 'Sorry to bother you' is a polite opening before a small request.
usage: Use it with strangers when you need a small favour.
leelaQ: Do you carry a pen with you every day?
answer: Yes, I always keep a pen in my bag.

en: It has been ages since we met! How are you?
tamil: நாம சந்திச்சு பல வருஷமாச்சு! எப்படி இருக்கீங்க?
context: Meeting an old school friend by chance.
explain: 'Ages' means a very long time. It is used in spoken English.
usage: Say it when you unexpectedly meet someone after many years.
leelaQ: Whom did you meet after a long time recently?
answer: I met my school friend at the bus stand.

en: Let's exchange numbers so we can plan a meetup.
tamil: நம்பர் மாத்திக்கலாம், அப்புறம் சந்திக்க திட்டம் போடலாம்.
context: Getting a new friend's phone number.
explain: 'Let's' is used to make a suggestion for both of you.
usage: Use it when you like a new person and want to meet again.
leelaQ: How many contacts do you have on your phone?
answer: I have around two hundred contacts.

en: What kind of work do you do?
tamil: நீங்க என்ன மாதிரி வேலை செய்யறீங்க?
context: Making small talk with a new acquaintance.
explain: 'What kind of' asks about the type of something. It sounds friendly, not pushy.
usage: Ask it casually when you meet someone for the first time.
leelaQ: What kind of work do you do and do you enjoy it?
answer: I work in an office and I enjoy it.

en: I work in a software company near the airport.
tamil: நான் விமான நிலையம் பக்கத்துல ஒரு சாஃப்ட்வேர் கம்பெனியில வேலை பாக்கறேன்.
context: Telling a new person about your job.
explain: 'Work in' is used for a company or field; 'work at' for a place.
usage: Say it when someone asks about your job at a party.
leelaQ: Where is your office and how do you go there?
answer: My office is near the station and I go by bus.

en: You two must come over for tea this evening.
tamil: நீங்க ரெண்டு பேரும் இன்னைக்கு சாயந்திரம் டீக்கு வீட்டுக்கு வரணும்.
context: Inviting neighbours to your home.
explain: 'Come over' means to visit someone's home. 'Must' makes the invitation warm.
usage: Use it to invite close neighbours or friends for a casual visit.
leelaQ: Do you like drinking tea in the evening?
answer: Yes, I always drink tea at five o'clock.

en: We'll definitely come to your daughter's engagement.
tamil: உங்க பொண்ணோட நிச்சயதார்த்தத்துக்கு நிச்சயம் வருவோம்.
context: Accepting an invitation from a colleague.
explain: 'Definitely' shows you are very sure about coming.
usage: Say it to promise a friend or colleague that you will attend.
leelaQ: Do you always keep your promise to attend functions?
answer: Yes, I try my best to attend every function.

en: I'm sorry, we already have another function that day.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், அன்னைக்கு எங்களுக்கு வேற ஒரு விழா இருக்கு.
context: Declining a wedding invitation politely.
explain: Giving a short reason makes a refusal polite.
usage: Say it when you cannot go to a function because of another plan.
leelaQ: What do you do if two functions come on the same day?
answer: I go to the closer relative's function first.

en: Would you mind taking a photo of all of us?
tamil: எங்க எல்லாரையும் ஒரு போட்டோ எடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a stranger to take a group photo.
explain: 'Would you mind...ing' is a very polite request form.
usage: Use it with strangers at a tourist place or a function.
leelaQ: Do you like taking photos at functions?
answer: Yes, I love taking photos with my family.

en: Everyone loved your speech at the reception.
tamil: வரவேற்புல நீங்க பேசினது எல்லாருக்கும் ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருந்துச்சு.
context: Praising a friend after his speech.
explain: 'Loved' is a stronger word than 'liked'.
usage: Say it to a person who spoke on stage and did well.
leelaQ: Can you speak confidently in front of a crowd?
answer: Not yet, but I am practising every day.

en: Thank you for coming all the way from Chennai.
tamil: சென்னையில இருந்து இவ்வளவு தூரம் வந்ததுக்கு நன்றி.
context: Thanking a relative who travelled far.
explain: 'All the way' stresses the long distance someone travelled.
usage: Say it to guests who have made a long trip for your function.
leelaQ: Which relative lives very far from your home?
answer: My uncle lives in Bangalore, very far from us.

en: I didn't recognise you at first. You've changed so much!
tamil: எனக்கு முதல்ல உங்களை அடையாளமே தெரியலை. நீங்க ரொம்ப மாறிட்டீங்க!
context: Meeting someone after many years.
explain: 'Recognise' means to know someone from before.
usage: Use it with old friends or relatives you meet after a long gap.
leelaQ: Has any friend of yours changed a lot over the years?
answer: Yes, my friend became much slimmer and more confident.

en: Make sure you give my regards to your parents.
tamil: உங்க அம்மா அப்பாகிட்ட என் வணக்கத்தை சொல்லுங்க.
context: Saying goodbye to a friend.
explain: 'Give my regards to' is a polite way to send greetings.
usage: Say it at the end of a chat when you want to greet someone's family.
leelaQ: How are your parents and what do they do?
answer: They are fine and they enjoy gardening.

en: Are you enjoying the party so far?
tamil: இதுவரைக்கும் பார்ட்டியை எஞ்சாய் பண்றீங்களா?
context: Checking on a guest at your party.
explain: 'So far' means until now.
usage: Ask it to a guest to show care as a host.
leelaQ: What do you enjoy most at a party?
answer: I enjoy the music and meeting new people.

en: I'm new to this city, so I don't know many people yet.
tamil: நான் இந்த ஊருக்கு புதுசு, அதனால இன்னும் நிறைய பேரை தெரியாது.
context: Telling a friendly colleague about yourself.
explain: 'Yet' is used in negatives to mean 'until now'.
usage: Use it to explain why you are alone when you move to a new place.
leelaQ: How do you make friends in a new city?
answer: I join a club and talk to my neighbours.

en: Let me introduce my friend Priya, she's visiting from Coimbatore.
tamil: என் தோழி பிரியாவை அறிமுகப்படுத்தறேன், அவ கோயம்புத்தூர்ல இருந்து வந்திருக்கா.
context: Introducing a friend to your colleagues.
explain: 'Let me introduce' is a formal and polite way to bring in a new person.
usage: Use it when you bring a friend to a group of people.
leelaQ: Who did you introduce to your family last?
answer: I introduced my best friend to my parents.

en: I was so nervous about meeting her parents for the first time.
tamil: அவளோட அம்மா அப்பாவை முதல் தடவை பாக்க எனக்கு ரொம்ப பதட்டமா இருந்துச்சு.
context: Telling a friend about a nervous experience.
explain: 'Nervous about' + an -ing word shows worry about a future event.
usage: Say it when you share your feelings about a big meeting.
leelaQ: What makes you nervous when you meet new people?
answer: I get nervous when I have to speak first.

en: Please accept this small gift as a token of my thanks.
tamil: என் நன்றியோட அடையாளமா இந்த சின்ன பரிசை ஏத்துக்கோங்க.
context: Giving a gift to someone who helped you.
explain: 'A token of' means a small sign of a feeling.
usage: Say it when you hand over a thank-you gift to a helper or teacher.
leelaQ: Whom would you like to give a thank-you gift?
answer: I would like to thank my teacher with a gift.

en: My family is going to visit your village next month.
tamil: என் குடும்பம் அடுத்த மாசம் உங்க கிராமத்துக்கு வரப்போறோம்.
context: Telling a friend about a planned visit.
explain: 'Going to' is used for plans you have already decided.
usage: Say it to a friend or relative when you plan to meet them.
leelaQ: Which village or town would you like to visit?
answer: I would like to visit a hill station in the summer.

en: What a lovely surprise! I never expected to see you here.
tamil: என்ன ஒரு இனிய ஆச்சரியம்! உங்களை இங்க பாப்பேன்னு நான் நினைக்கவே இல்லை.
context: Meeting a friend unexpectedly in a mall.
explain: 'Never expected' shows complete surprise. 'What a...' shows strong feeling.
usage: Use it when you meet a known person in an unexpected place.
leelaQ: Have you ever met a friend in a surprising place?
answer: Yes, I once met my cousin at the airport.

en: Do join us if you are free this Sunday.
tamil: இந்த ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமை உங்களுக்கு நேரமிருந்தா எங்களோட சேருங்க.
context: Giving a casual invite to a neighbour.
explain: 'Do' before a verb makes a request warm and strong.
usage: Use it to invite someone in a friendly, no-pressure way.
leelaQ: What do you usually do on Sunday?
answer: I relax at home and meet my friends.

en: That is a lovely saree. The colour suits you very well.
tamil: அது அழகான புடவை. அந்த நிறம் உங்களுக்கு ரொம்ப பொருத்தமா இருக்கு.
context: Complimenting a relative at a wedding.
explain: 'Suits you' means looks good on you. It is a polite way to praise someone.
usage: Say it to a woman at a wedding or festival to praise her dress.
leelaQ: Whose dress did you praise at the last function?
answer: I praised my cousin's saree at her friend's wedding.

en: We are inviting everyone for my sister's engagement next Sunday.
tamil: அடுத்த ஞாயிற்றுக்கிழமை என் தங்கை நிச்சயதார்த்தத்துக்கு எல்லாரையும் கூப்பிடறோம்.
context: Inviting a neighbour to a family function.
explain: Present continuous with 'next Sunday' talks about a planned event.
usage: Use it when you personally invite neighbours or friends to a family event.
leelaQ: Who will you invite to the next family function?
answer: I will invite my neighbours and close friends.
